chapters.summary: Chair Eric Dinowitz opens the Education Committee vote, acknowledging colleagues present including Councilmembers Louis, Narcisse, Lee, Joseph, Farías, Schulman, De La Rosa, and Wong.
chapters.title: Chair Dinowitz opens Education Committee vote and acknowledges members present

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Eric Dinowitz, Chair of the Committee on Education.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Welcome to today's vote.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: First, I want to acknowledge my colleagues who are present, Councilmembers Lewis, Narcisse, Lee, Joseph, Arias, Shulman, De La Rosa, and Wong.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz introduces proposed Resolution 7A, sponsored by Councilmembers Ariola, Speaker Menin, and Joseph, calling on the State Legislature and Governor to require a 9/11 curriculum in all New York schools, noting the upcoming 25th anniversary.
chapters.title: Dinowitz introduces Resolution 7A calling for statewide 9/11 curriculum

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Today the Committee on Education will consider proposed Resolution 7A, sponsored by Council Members Joann-Ariola, Speaker Julie-Menin, and Council Member Rita Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The resolution calls on the New York State Legislature to pass and the Governor to sign legislation to incorporate a 9-11 curriculum in all New York City schools.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: This Friday marks the 25th anniversary of the September 11th terrorist attack against the United States.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz recounts the September 11 attacks—19 hijackers, four planes, nearly 3,000 killed, 6,000 injured—and describes how the events transformed American attitudes about safety, privacy, and global affairs, with impacts still felt in New York City today.
chapters.title: Dinowitz recounts the events and lasting impact of September 11, 2001

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: On that day in 2001, 19 terrorists hijacked four commercial planes, deliberately crashing two of the planes into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center here in New York City, a less than 10 minute walk from where we are now.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Nearly 3,000 people were killed and more than 6,000 others were injured, not to mention the countless

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: less others who have died from 9-11 related illnesses.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The events of 9-11 transformed Americans'attitudes about safety, privacy, and our nation's role in global affairs,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: the impacts of which are still felt today, including again here in New York City where survivors, first responders, residents, and family members and neighbors continue to deal with the effects of that horrific day.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz explains that for today's students, 9/11 is a historical event with uneven classroom coverage and no required curriculum. He notes the sensitivity of the material and the need for age-appropriate, intentionally crafted instruction.
chapters.title: Dinowitz explains why students need a structured 9/11 curriculum

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: While 9-11 and the events that followed are ingrained memories for many adults, many of us sitting here today,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: for students in our schools, 9-11 is a historical event that can receive uneven coverage in classes, as there is currently no required curriculum that covers it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Whether and how students learn about 9-11 can vary depending on the teacher and the school.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Teaching this topic can be a delicate task, as the material is sensitive and the images and documents used as primary sources can be disturbing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: An important topic such as this one deserves the kind of careful, age-appropriate consideration that can come from an intentionally crafted curriculum.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz describes how Resolution 7A proposes state legislation requiring an age-appropriate 9/11 curriculum covering core events and global impact, emphasizing that New York City students must learn this history to understand today's world.
chapters.title: Dinowitz outlines what Resolution 7A would require

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Resolution 7A proposes state legislation that would require 9-11 curriculum be age-appropriate and include certain core information and themes on the events of the day and the global impact of the attacks.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It is critical that New York City students learn about

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: 9-11 to better understand today's world and our city's history.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And that is precisely what proposed Resolution 7A seeks to ensure.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Therefore, I ask my colleagues to support this resolution.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I would now like to turn it over to one of the bill's sponsors, Councilmember Joseph, for some remarks.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Rita Joseph recalls being a fifth-grade teacher on 9/11, watching the towers fall on live TV with her class, and learning that one student's father who worked at Windows on the World was off that day but lost coworkers. She describes carrying that morning with her throughout her career.
chapters.title: Councilmember Joseph recalls teaching 5th grade on 9/11 and watching the towers fall

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Dinowitz.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The resolution 7A calling on Albany to pass the governor to sign legislation requiring a 9-11 curriculum in every school in the state.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Let me tell you where I was.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I was a fifth grade teacher.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: My students were 10 years old.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: This week marks 25 years since that day, which means those 10-year-olds are now grown.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: They are in their 30s, some of them raising their own children, children who will never know September 11 as history the way I knew Pearl Harbor.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I remember exactly where I was, room 303.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The principal came over the PA system and said, turn on your TVs, something is happening.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We turned on our television and my whole class watched the towers fall, live together right here in that classroom.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: One of my students had a father who worked at the windows on the world, at the top of the North Tower.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I remember calling to find out if that family was okay.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: When I reached him, he told me he happened to be off that day.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: He was safe, but I could hear it in his voice.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: He had tears in his eyes because he was thinking about his coworkers, the people he worked beside every single day.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Who weren't.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: It's so fortunate.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I carry that morning with me for the rest of the career in that classroom.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I think about it every time I stand in this chamber and talk about what our students need to know.

chapters.summary: Joseph argues that a moment of silence is not enough—curriculum teaches. She notes that today's teachers and students weren't alive for 9/11, references existing NYC DOE resources and museum visits, and calls for statewide legislation so children in Buffalo and Rochester learn this history with the same seriousness as those in Brooklyn.
chapters.title: Joseph argues moment of silence is not enough and urges statewide 9/11 curriculum

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: New York already requires moment of silence in our schools each September 11th.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That matters, but a moment of silence is not a lesson plan.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Silence remembers, curriculum teaches.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: My generation of teachers didn't need a curriculum to explain that day, we lived it.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And we improvised because we had to.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: But the teachers standing in front of the classrooms today weren't there, neither were their students.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: If we don't require this history to be taught deliberately and well, it simply won't be.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Not due to a lack of care, but because people who remember it firsthand were getting fewer every year.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: New York City has tried to close that gap.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Our Department of Education built 911 curriculum resources with the Memorial Museum, and this council funded students'visit to the museum this year.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: But a child in Buffalo or Rochester deserves to learn this history with the same seriousness as a child in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That's statewide responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: State lawmakers have introduced legislation to do exactly that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Firefighter Joseph Spar Jr., who responded to Rescue 3 that morning and never came home.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Resolution 7A tells Albany that the City Council stand behind that effort.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I want to thank my colleagues for years of working and keeping this history alive, for the generation that wasn't there to witness it.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I urge my colleague to vote yes.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I urge Albany to act.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz thanks Councilmember Brewer for years of work on 9/11 family justice, notes additional members joining (Gutierrez, Salazar), and thanks committee staff including Alejandro Carvajal, Chloe Rivera, Katie Selena, Grace Amato, Andrew Lane Lawless, and his own staff Theo Solter and Jenna Klaus.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'd also like to note that we've been joined by Councilmember Brewer, who has been instrumental in justice for the 9-11 families for many, many years.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I've been joined by Councilmember Gutierrez and Council Girl Salazar Gutierrez.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Finally, I want to thank committee staff Alejandro Carvajal, Chloe Rivera, Katie Selena, Grace Amato, Andrew Lane Lawless, as well as my own staff, Theo Solter and Jenna Klaus.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Clerk, we are ready to begin the vote.

summary: The NYC Council Committee on Education held a vote on Resolution 7A, calling on the State Legislature and Governor to require an age-appropriate 9/11 curriculum in all New York schools.
Chair Eric Dinowitz and sponsor Councilmember Rita Joseph delivered remarks on the importance of teaching 9/11 history, with Joseph sharing her personal experience as a teacher on that day.
The resolution was adopted by a vote of 12-0, with one member voting late after the initial roll call.
title: Committee on Education
topic: Incorporate a 9/11 curriculum in all New York schools. (A.8347)
